title: TIFR Scientist Ankona Datta Wins James Hoeschele Award for Biological Inorganic Chemistry
excerpt: The TIFR Mumbai professor, whose group builds sensors that make metal ions visible inside living cells, becomes the second Indian winner of the Asia-Pacific mid-career award.
body:
• Professor Ankona Datta of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), Mumbai, has won the James Hoeschele AsBIC Award for outstanding research in biological inorganic chemistry, India Today reported.
  • The award, established in 2018, honours mid-career scientists in the Asia-Pacific region and is presented every alternate year with a US$500 prize and an award lecture at the next AsBIC conference.
  • Datta's Chemical Biology and Molecular Imaging group at TIFR builds fluorescent and Raman sensors that make metal ions and other biomolecules visible inside living cells.
  • She is the second Indian winner of the award, after IACS professor Abhishek Dey in 2022.

Professor Ankona Datta, a chemist at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) in Mumbai, has won the James Hoeschele AsBIC Award for her research in biological inorganic chemistry, India Today reported on Friday. The award is given by the Asian Society of Biological Inorganic Chemistry (AsBIC).

An Award for Mid-Career Scientists

The James Hoeschele AsBIC Award was established in 2018 with support from Professor James Hoeschele of Eastern Michigan University, the co-inventor of the cancer drug carboplatin. According to the Society of Biological Inorganic Chemistry's awards page, it recognises outstanding scientific contributions in biological inorganic chemistry by mid-career researchers in the Asia-Pacific region, and aims to strengthen collaboration within that community. Up to two awards are presented every alternate year, each carrying a cash prize of US$500 and a certificate, and recipients are invited to deliver an award lecture at the next AsBIC conference.

Datta follows a short list of previous winners: Mi Hee Lim and Jun-Long Zhang in 2020, Abhishek Dey of the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science and Shigeyuki Masaoka in 2022, and Guangyu Zhu and Jaeheung Cho in 2024. Dey remains the only previous Indian recipient.

Sensors That Light Up Inside Living Cells

Datta leads the Chemical Biology and Molecular Imaging group in TIFR's Department of Chemical Sciences. Her group's work, described on its TIFR research pages, centres on chemical tools that let scientists watch biology happen in real time: fluorescent probes that image phosphoinositides, signalling lipids in cell membranes; copper chelators that bind copper at picomolar affinity and slow the production of damaging hydroxyl radicals; and small-molecule ratiometric sensors that track autophagy, the cell's recycling machinery, in living systems.

More recent work from the group includes "morphable stitched" sensors designed to image several biomolecules at once in living cells, published in JACS Au, and activity-based Raman sensors intended to visualise elusive species such as hydrogen peroxide and copper ions. The common thread is biological inorganic chemistry's central question: how metal ions behave inside cells, and what goes wrong when that behaviour is disturbed in diseases involving oxidative stress, cancer and neurodegeneration.

Why the Recognition Matters

Biological inorganic chemistry sits between chemistry, biology and medicine, and its Asia-Pacific community is small enough that the Hoeschele award functions as a marker of the researchers shaping the field's direction. For TIFR, the win adds to a run of international recognition for Indian fundamental science at a moment when the institute's chemical sciences department is also pushing its research into classrooms, with faculty workshops planned for college chemistry teachers this November.

Datta will receive the prize and deliver her award lecture at the next AsBIC conference, alongside up to one other recipient for this cycle.
